title: Katzmann: Congress and the lawmaking process (pp. 11–22)
shortTitle: Katzmann: Congress and the lawmaking process (pp. 11–22)
summary: Katzmann argues that understanding Congress’s actual procedures and division of labor improves interpretation of its statutes.
notes:
Katzmann begins with institutional interdependence: the Constitution distributes powers but leaves Congress substantial freedom to develop internal lawmaking procedures. Committees organize expertise, attention, and bargaining. Authorizing committees shape programs and policy, appropriations committees control spending and its conditions, and oversight examines implementation. Staff and professional legislative counsel perform much drafting, while leaders, executive officials, and outside groups also participate.

Multiple decision points, competing jurisdictions, time pressure, coalition building, and deliberate compromise can produce ambiguity. Omnibus legislation packages different measures for an up-or-down decision, so support for an entire bill does not show that every legislator endorses every provision. Drafting on the floor or late in conference can bypass technical review. Katzmann’s numerical examples describe Congresses around 2009–2012 and should not be represented as current statistics.

Members rely on committee reports, conference reports, and colleagues managing legislation because they cannot personally master every detail. Amendatory language can be hard to understand without knowing the existing code; the Hobby Protection Act example illustrates that problem. Katzmann argues that reputation and continuing institutional relationships give staff and committee leaders incentives to describe bills accurately. These observations support his later claim that reliable legislative materials can help courts identify congressional meaning. They also leave room for error, strategic drafting, and disagreement.
